newsitem.title: USA: U.S. experts say dlr to gain now EMU back on track.
newsitem.headline: U.S. experts say dlr to gain now EMU back on track.

text.p: Agreement over the European Union stability pact removes only one of many obstacles littering the path toward monetary union which ultimately will weaken the euro and strengthen the dollar, U.S. analysts said on Monday.

The dollar's reaction was muted to news on Monday that EU finance ministers clinched agreement on a pact that will link budget discipline among members of the bloc's planned single currency to growth and jobs.
The market had already celebrated the news on Friday in its classic "buy the rumor, sell the fact" style.

The dollar pushed above 1.74 marks on Friday, but fell short of its 39-month high of 1.7423 marks hit on June 6, as market makers bet correctly that EU leaders would reach an agreement at their two-day Amsterdam summit.

The deal put to bed the latest crisis in unification plans which erupted last week when France's new Socialist government held up the routine agreement of the stability pact, which it said did nothing to aid the bloc's jobless problem.
On Monday, the dollar slid in early trade despite news of the pact as dealers unwound long positions to book profits after the dollar rally faltered over the weekend.

"The fact that they reached an agreement was hinted at in the Franco-German summit on Friday when both sides suggested an agreement was possible. It didn't come as too much of a surprise today," said Bob Lynch, currency strategist at Banque Paribas in New York.
"The fact that the mark has actually firmed against the dollar but softened against some of the European crosses shows a mixed reaction and nothing special on the news," he added.
Another reason the dollar lost ground on Monday was the stability pact was not noticeably watered down by the newly formed resolutions for employment and economic growth.

"The agreement leans more heavily toward the German position than the French position in the sense that we are not talking about either diluting the stability pact or taking a significant addition to the European budget in order to get the French to compromise," said John Rothfield, international economist at Nationsbanc.

"The French may be making some kind of face saving compromise so that the prime minister can go back and tell the National Assembly that there is a more humane element to the treaty. They haven't really got that much when it all comes down to it," he added.

However, most analysts said the dollar will be the ultimate beneficiary in the drive to monetary union as fiscal criteria will have to be loosened and a broader base of countries would then qualify for first-round membership.
"I still think EMU will go ahead but there will be some fudging on the criteria and that will be taken as negative by the market," said Chris Iggo, international economist at BZW Securities Inc.
"There's a lot to do between now and next spring when they choose which countries will be let in," he added.
Ron Leven, currency strategist at JP Morgan, agreed and said that all facts point to "the broad euro, weak euro scenario."
